question.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the $8$-periodic extension of the function $F(x)=\frac{3}{2}x$ defined on $[-4,4).$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below, showing the derivation of a series converging to the $8$-periodic extension of 

$$
G(x)=\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}={\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x).$

The Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
\frac{3}{2}x∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }{{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f$ is 
{{field-2}} 
on $R,$ we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term to get

$$
\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{{field-3}}\cdot {{field-4}}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $F(x)$ is an odd function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=4$ and we are already given the coefficients ${b}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4}).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-4,4).$ 
Therefore, the $8$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{3}{2}t\,\text{d}t & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{12(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{4})\,\text{d}t \\ {[\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{x} & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\cdot [-\frac{4}{n\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{4})]_{0}^{x} \\ \frac{3}{4}{x}^{2} & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{48(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\cdot (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4}))\end{aligned}
$$
